hops.title: Why lactose-free milk tastes sweeter
hops.text: Plain lactose-free milk often tastes sweeter than regular milk, though nobody added sugar. Milk's own sugar, lactose, is a double sugar: one glucose and one galactose joined by a single link. Many people make less lactase, the enzyme that splits it, after infancy, so the dairy adds lactase for them, and sometimes the splitting finishes after the carton is sealed. Hydrolysis puts one water into each link it breaks, turning each lactose into a glucose plus a galactose. Each single sugar tastes sweeter than the pair did.

hops.title: The survey where most people wanted DNA labels on food
hops.text: In a 2015 survey of 1,004 Americans, researchers Brandon McFadden and Jayson Lusk found that 80 percent wanted mandatory labels on foods containing DNA. That reaction makes sense; DNA sounds like something from a crime lab, not a lunchbox. The catch is that almost any food made from plant or animal cells carries their DNA, so the label would go on strawberries, whole-wheat bread and the turkey in your sandwich. Your gut simply takes food DNA apart, just as it takes apart starch and protein.

hops.title: The copper box behind the 4 and the 9
hops.text: In 1892, Wesleyan's Wilbur Atwater and Edward Rosa began building a copper-walled box about 6 feet high, 4 wide and 7 long. Students and a lab janitor nicknamed "Swede" Osterberg lived inside for days, resting, exercising and eating, while the team measured the carbon dioxide and heat they gave off. The box showed energy conservation holds for people too. For food energy, the team burned foods, then subtracted what people fail to absorb and the protein energy lost in urine. Rounded, these mixed-diet averages give this page's 4 and 9.

audio.title: A panda, a camel and a box of used bandages
audio.transcript:
Let's visit a panda, a camel and a castle cellar, because each one shows a big molecule doing its job, or refusing to.

Start with the giant panda. A panda can spend ten to sixteen hours a day eating, sitting upright on the ground like a person on the floor, holding each stalk with a kind of extra thumb that is really an enlarged wrist bone. It can get through about twelve and a half kilograms of bamboo in a day. And yet, in feeding trials with two captive pandas, researchers estimated that the animals digested less than a fifth of the bamboo's dry matter, and only about eight percent of its cellulose. Most of it simply passes through. Here is why. Cellulose is a chain of glucose, the same sugar that makes up the starch in a potato. But cellulose's glucose blocks are joined by a different kind of link, and the panda's own enzymes cannot cut it. Its gut is built more like a meat eater's, and its gut bacteria look more like a meat eater's too, with few of the kinds that break down cellulose. So the panda sits on a pile of glucose it mostly cannot unlock, and makes up for it by eating a great deal of bamboo and moving it through quickly.

Next, the camel. You have probably heard that a camel's hump is a water tank. It is not. A hump is mostly fat, and the Cleveland Zoo says a single hump can hold up to eighty pounds of it. That is fat doing exactly the job in your lesson table: long-term energy storage. When food runs short, the camel breaks down hump fat for energy, and the hump shrinks. After long hunger it can nearly disappear. On adult domestic Bactrian camels, the two-humped kind, a hump can go soft and flop over to one side, which looks a little undignified. Keeping the fat in one place has a desert bonus, too: the rest of the body is not wrapped in a warm coat of fat. And the water? Camels are simply excellent drinkers. A thirsty one can drink about thirty gallons in ten minutes.

Last, a castle in Tübingen, Germany, in eighteen sixty-nine. A twenty-four-year-old Swiss scientist named Friedrich Miescher had a lab in the castle's old vaults, and he wanted to know what white blood cells are made of. Where do you find a lot of white blood cells? In pus. So the local hospital sent him its used bandages. He had to invent his own ways to get the cells off the bandages and pull them apart. Out came a substance that was not protein and not fat. It was acidic, and it was much richer in phosphorus than proteins are. That phosphorus is the P in your lesson's table, in the row for nucleic acids. Because it came from the cell's nucleus, he called it nuclein. His sample was not pure, but its main ingredient is what we now call D N A. Miescher later wondered whether nuclein played a part in fertilization and heredity. About seventy-five years after he found it, experiments in nineteen forty-four showed that D N A could pass a trait from one bacterium to another.

One sugar locked behind the wrong link, one fat tucked into a hump, and one acid hiding in a bandage. Each time, the blocks and the way they are put together decided what the molecule could do.
